title: How a studio estimates a marketing site
metaTitle: What sets a marketing site's cost
excerpt: A marketing site's cost follows templates, states, copy you still have to write, and whether a shop or a product is in scope. A page count alone is a guess.

faqs.question: Why is a page count a weak way to price a site?
faqs.answer: Five entries that share a template are one design and five content jobs, not five designs. A custom calculator, a shop, or a login is its own line. States such as empty, error, and sold out multiply a template even when the URL count stays the same. Price the list of templates and states, not the sitemap sketch.

faqs.question: How should missing copy affect the estimate?
faqs.answer: Name who writes the headlines and the key pages, how many rounds are included, and what happens if the words arrive late. A build that waits on a manifesto burns the days you thought were for engineering. Existing photography should be opened and judged before anyone calls it done.

faqs.question: What should you ask a studio to show in the quote?
faqs.answer: Ask for templates, states, the content owner, whether a shop or a product is included, the integrations, the rounds of feedback, and the exclusions. A single line that says design and development cannot be compared with another studio's number. You would be comparing slogans.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Website design cost factors are the things a page count hides: how many templates you actually need, how many states each one has, whether the words exist yet, and whether a shop or a product is in scope. A quote that starts from “about ten pages” is a guess with a professional font. The number of URLs is the smallest part of the work.

Ask what the site must do for a stranger, then list the screens that job requires. The cost follows that list. It does not follow a sitemap someone sketched in a kickoff and never edited.

## Templates, not pages

A template is a layout with rules, used by many entries or by one important screen. A homepage, a case-study template, a product template, an article template. Five case studies that share a template are not five designs. They are one design and five content jobs. Price them that way, or you will argue later about what “a page” included.

Unique screens cost more than repeated ones. A custom calculator, a configurator, a map of stockists, a logged-in portal. If it is not a template you already have, it is its own line. Say so in the estimate. A footer link labeled “portal” can hide a product.

States multiply a template. Empty, loading, error, success, signed-out, sold-out, mobile nav open. A product page with variants and an unavailable state is a larger object than a product page that assumes the happy path. The notes for those states are part of the design, and the components are part of the build. Leaving them out of the quote does not leave them out of the project. It leaves them out of the schedule until they appear as “small tweaks.”

Write the template list in the estimate, with a one-line job for each. “Article: title, date, body, one image style, related posts.” If you cannot write the line, you do not yet know the cost. Go back to the job the page performs.

## Words and pictures you still have to make

Copy is a cost even when the founder will “just write it.” A homepage that must be understood in the first seconds needs a headline, a supporting sentence, and proof. Nielsen Norman Group’s 2011 article on [how long users stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) makes the practical point: people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a clear value proposition in the first 10 seconds is what earns longer attention. Drafting that proposition is work. So is rewriting it when the first version could describe any studio on earth.

If the words do not exist, the estimate should say who writes them, how many rounds you include, and what happens if they arrive late. A build that waits on a manifesto will burn the days you thought were for engineering. A build that invents the manifesto will burn trust.

Photography and illustration are the same kind of line. Existing assets, a small art direction, or a new set. “We’ll use what’s in the drive” is not a plan until someone has opened the drive and named the files that are good enough. Weak images make a designed template look unfinished, and the redesign of the images becomes an unpaid phase.

Translation, legal review, and product data are content too. A shop with 200 SKUs and no clean names is a content project that looks like a theme install. Put the data work in the estimate or cut the catalog to what is clean.

## A shop or a product changes the shape

A marketing site is a set of templates, a form, and a way to edit. An ecommerce migration adds catalog, bag, checkout, shipping copy, returns, and the states where an item is gone. Those are not “a few more pages.” Down the Cove’s public project is an ecommerce migration and redesign, which is a different scope from a calm brand site such as Wabisabi, or a community sports site such as Ballarat Box Sports.

A product interface is another scope again. Got Next and Leadly are public product interfaces. Trade Moai is a trading interface concept. They need flows, permissions, empty states, and an account, which a homepage estimate does not cover. If the founder says “and the app, basically the same brand,” split the quote. One brand system can serve both. One number cannot, without someone absorbing the surprise.

Integrations are scope. A payment provider, a booking tool, a CMS, an analytics setup, a migration from a platform you still have to export. Each one has an unknown until you have seen the current account. Price a discovery spike if you have not seen it, rather than a fixed line that pretends you have.

The CMS choice changes the cost in a specific way. Editing a few templates in a structured editor is one job. A page builder that lets every section be reinvented is a different, longer support burden. Say which one the quote assumes. Hanabi’s marketing builds are code, Next.js and React, with structured content where the team needs to edit. That assumption should be visible in the estimate so nobody expects a blank canvas of blocks.

## Rounds, review, and the things people forget

Design rounds are a cost. Two rounds of feedback on the key templates is a different project from unlimited revision until everyone is tired. Name the rounds. Name who may send feedback. A committee that arrives in round three with a new audience is a new estimate, not a use of the old one.

Implementation includes the unglamorous list. Domain and DNS, analytics, a staging site, redirects if you are replacing a live site, basic metadata, a form that actually notifies a person, and a pass on type size and focus states. None of these are a page. All of them are how a launch stops being a screenshot.

Performance is a requirement, not a mood. A marketing page still has to load and stay still while it loads. If the quote includes heavy video, custom motion, or a large library of third-party scripts, say what you will measure and what you will refuse to add. Discovering ten chat widgets in week four is a change of scope.

Accessibility is the same kind of line. A serious pass on labels, contrast, focus, and errors takes time. “We’ll make it accessible” with no tasks is a wish. List the tasks you include, and list what you do not, such as a formal audit.

Launch support is easy to forget because it feels like it should be free. The week the DNS moves is when the form breaks, the font fails, or the redirect map is short. Include a defined window of fixes for defects against the agreed templates. New ideas in that window are a new quote.

## How to read an estimate without a page-count argument

Ask for the list. Templates, states, content owner, shop or product, integrations, rounds, and the launch window. If a line says “design and development” and nothing else, you cannot compare it to another studio’s number. You are comparing slogans.

Ask what would change the number. More templates, a shop, a product login, copy written by the studio, a migration with redirects. A studio that can answer that list understands the work. A studio that says the number is the number, until it is not, will discover the scope with your launch date.

Ask what you will own. The repository, the CMS logins, the type and color decisions, the ability to edit the pages you were promised. Code ownership is part of the cost conversation because a cheap build you cannot run is not cheap.

Do not ask a studio to match a number from a template marketplace. The marketplace sold a theme. You are buying a set of decisions and a codebase your team can keep. Those are different products. Compare them on the list, not on the sticker.

A useful estimate fits on a few pages and still names the exclusions. “Not included: photography, copywriting beyond two headline rounds, native apps, paid ads.” Exclusions are a kindness. They are how a fixed number stays fixed.

## Bring a draft list to the first conversation

Before you ask for a number, write your own template list and mark what content exists. You will be wrong in places. That is fine. The wrong list is a better start than “we need a website,” because it gives the studio something to correct.

Bring the current site and one competitor you respect, plus one you do not want to resemble. Say whether a shop or a product login is in the next six months. If it is, say so now. Adding it after the templates are designed is the expensive way to reveal it. If you are unsure, ask for two estimates side by side, marketing site alone and marketing site plus the shop or the login, so the difference is a number you chose rather than a surprise.

The shape of the agreement matters as much as the ingredients. [What flexible means on a fixed project](/blog/what-flexible-means-on-a-fixed-project) is the next piece. It is about which changes the number still absorbs, and which ones mean you are buying a different project.

When you want that list turned into a real range, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the templates you think you need. The call is for testing the list, not for sending a surprise invoice.
